notes.definition: Global warming is the increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface. Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing, and these gases contribute to global warming, which has many biological consequences.
explanation: Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases. They let energy from the Sun reach the Earth's surface but absorb some of the energy that the warmed Earth radiates back out, which keeps the Earth warmer than it would otherwise be. The levels of both gases in the atmosphere are increasing. Carbon dioxide has risen mainly because of burning fossil fuels and deforestation (burning trees, decay of wood and less photosynthesis). Methane has risen because of cattle farming, rice fields and the decay of waste in landfill sites. Higher concentrations of these gases contribute to global warming.

The evidence for global warming comes from many sources, including direct measurements of carbon dioxide since the 1950s, temperature records, and air bubbles trapped in ancient ice. Scientists agree that recent warming is linked to human activities because of a very large body of peer-reviewed evidence. However, the climate is a very complex system, so predictions of exactly how much warming will happen, and its effects in particular places, are uncertain.

Global warming has biological consequences. Rising temperatures cause ice to melt and sea water to expand, so sea levels rise. Low-lying coastal areas such as salt marshes, mangroves and some islands may be flooded, causing loss of habitat for the species that live there. Melting sea ice removes the habitat that animals such as polar bears and seals use for hunting and breeding.

Changes in temperature and rainfall change the distribution of species. Many species are found further towards the poles or at higher altitudes as the areas they used to live in become too warm. Species that need cool conditions may have nowhere to go. Some species, including pests and organisms that carry diseases (such as some mosquitoes), may spread into new areas where it used to be too cold for them, which can affect crops, livestock and human health.

Global warming changes migration patterns. Some birds arrive earlier in spring, some stop migrating altogether, and others change their routes. The timing of events such as flowering, leaf growth and insect emergence also changes. If a bird's chicks hatch after the peak in the caterpillars they feed on, fewer chicks survive. When species cannot adapt or move fast enough, populations fall and some species may become extinct, so biodiversity is reduced.
keyFacts: Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing.
Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases that contribute to global warming.
Burning fossil fuels and deforestation increase carbon dioxide levels.
Cattle, rice fields and landfill increase methane levels.
Rising sea levels flood low-lying areas, causing loss of habitat.
Changes in temperature and rainfall change the distribution of species.
Migration patterns and the timing of seasonal events are changing.
Biodiversity may be reduced as species that cannot adapt or move die out.
The climate is a complex system, so predictions about global warming involve uncertainty.

keyTerms.definition: The increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide or methane, that absorbs energy radiated from the Earth's surface and so keeps the Earth warm.
A greenhouse gas (CO₂) released by combustion and respiration and removed by photosynthesis.
A greenhouse gas (CH₄) released by cattle, rice fields and decaying waste in landfill.
The seasonal movement of animals from one area to another, for example to breed or find food.
The increase in the average height of the sea, caused by melting ice on land and the expansion of warmer sea water.
The checking of a scientist's work by other experts before it is published.

equations.name: Percentage change
equations.formula: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100

workedExamples.question: Use the graph in the notes. Atmospheric carbon dioxide was 317 ppm in 1960 and 414 ppm in 2020. Calculate the percentage increase. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

workedExamples.title: Mean rate of increase
workedExamples.question: Calculate the mean rate of increase of carbon dioxide concentration between 2000 (370 ppm) and 2020 (414 ppm).

workedExamples.title: Explaining a biological consequence
workedExamples.question: Explain how global warming could cause a species of saltmarsh plant to lose its habitat.
steps: Global warming melts ice on land and causes sea water to expand.
Low-lying saltmarshes are flooded more often or permanently, so the plant cannot survive there.
workedExamples.answer: Rising sea levels flood the low-lying saltmarsh, so its habitat is lost.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think global warming is caused by the hole in the ozone layer.
misconceptions.right: In fact, global warming is linked to increasing greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane. The ozone layer is a separate issue.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think global warming just means every place gets hotter every year.
misconceptions.right: In fact, it is a rise in the average temperature of the Earth; some places and years may be cooler, and rainfall patterns change too.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think carbon dioxide is the only greenhouse gas that matters.
misconceptions.right: In fact, methane is also increasing and is a powerful greenhouse gas; AQA names both.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think animals move because they choose to escape the heat.
misconceptions.right: In fact, distribution changes because populations survive and reproduce better in some places than others as conditions change.

realWorld: Many UK bird species now lay their eggs earlier in spring than they did 50 years ago.
Coral reefs suffer bleaching when sea temperatures rise, which can kill the coral and reduce reef biodiversity.
Polar bears depend on sea ice to hunt seals, and the loss of Arctic sea ice is reducing their hunting time.
Some insect pests and disease-carrying mosquitoes are spreading into regions that used to be too cold for them.
examTips: Name both gases: carbon dioxide and methane. Many students forget methane.
For 'describe biological consequences', give specific effects such as loss of habitat from flooding, changes in distribution, changes in migration patterns and reduced biodiversity.
Link each consequence back to the change that causes it (for example warming → ice melts → sea level rises → low-lying habitats flooded).
When reading graphs of carbon dioxide, check the scale: the vertical axis often does not start at zero.
Do not confuse global warming with ozone depletion or with acid rain.
summary: Carbon dioxide and methane levels in the atmosphere are increasing.
These gases contribute to global warming.
Rising sea levels flood low-lying areas, causing loss of habitat.
Species change their distribution as temperature and rainfall change.
Migration patterns and timing of seasonal events change.
Species that cannot adapt or move may die out, reducing biodiversity.

flashcards.front: Which two gases does AQA say are increasing and contribute to global warming?
Give two sources of extra carbon dioxide.
Give two sources of extra methane.
flashcards.back: Cattle and rice fields (also landfill sites).

flashcards.front: How does global warming cause loss of habitat?
flashcards.back: Ice melts and sea levels rise, flooding low-lying areas; sea ice is lost.

flashcards.front: How does global warming change species distribution?
flashcards.back: Species shift towards the poles or uphill; warm-adapted species spread into new areas.

flashcards.front: How can global warming affect migration?
flashcards.back: Birds may arrive earlier, change routes or stop migrating.

flashcards.front: Why might global warming reduce biodiversity?
flashcards.back: Species that cannot adapt or move fast enough die out.

flashcards.front: Name an organism that may spread into new areas with warming.
flashcards.back: For example disease-carrying mosquitoes or crop pests.
The climate is a complex system with many interacting factors.
The increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface.
About 317 ppm in 1960 and about 414 ppm in 2020.

flashcards.front: How can warming affect food chains through timing?
flashcards.back: Chicks may hatch after the peak in their insect food, so fewer survive.

questions.question: Which two gases are increasing in the atmosphere and contributing to global warming?
options: Oxygen and nitrogen
Sulfur dioxide and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and methane
Nitrogen and argon
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide and methane
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases. Oxygen, nitrogen and argon are not greenhouse gases, and sulfur dioxide is linked to acid rain.

questions.question: Which human activity releases methane into the atmosphere?
options: Planting trees
Cattle farming
Using solar panels
Recycling glass
markScheme: 1 mark: cattle farming
questions.explanation: Cattle produce methane during digestion. Planting trees removes carbon dioxide, and solar panels and recycling do not release methane.

questions.question: Global warming causes sea levels to rise. What is the most likely biological consequence?
options: Low-lying habitats are flooded and lost
All fish die
Mountain habitats are flooded
Deserts get wetter
markScheme: 1 mark: low-lying habitats are flooded and lost
questions.explanation: Rising seas flood low-lying coastal areas such as saltmarshes, mangroves and small islands.

questions.question: What does global warming mean?
options: An increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface
Every day being hotter than the day before
A hole in the ozone layer
An increase in the amount of rain
markScheme: 1 mark: an increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface
questions.explanation: Global warming is about the average temperature over the whole Earth. Individual days can still be cold, and the ozone layer is a separate issue.

questions.question: A butterfly species that used to be found only in southern England is now also found in Scotland. Which is the most likely explanation?
options: Butterflies have learned to fly further
Scotland has become colder
The butterflies were blown north by one storm
Global warming has made northern areas warm enough for the species to survive and breed
markScheme: 1 mark: warming means northern areas now suit the species
questions.explanation: As temperatures rise, areas further north become suitable, so the species' distribution spreads north.

questions.question: Which is a change in migration patterns that could be caused by global warming?
options: Birds growing longer feathers
Birds arriving in the UK earlier in spring
Birds laying blue eggs
Birds losing the ability to fly
markScheme: 1 mark: birds arriving earlier in spring
questions.explanation: Warmer springs can change the timing of migration. The other changes are not migration patterns.

questions.question: Why might global warming increase the spread of some diseases?
options: Warmer temperatures kill all pathogens
Global warming makes people immune to disease
Organisms that carry pathogens, such as mosquitoes, can survive in areas that used to be too cold
Carbon dioxide is a pathogen
markScheme: 1 mark: vectors such as mosquitoes can survive in new, previously cold areas
questions.explanation: Warmer conditions let vectors and pests spread into new areas. Warming does not kill all pathogens, and carbon dioxide is not a pathogen.

questions.question: A species of alpine plant grows only near the tops of mountains. Why is it particularly at risk from global warming?
options: It will grow too fast in warm conditions
Its cool habitat moves uphill and it has nowhere higher to move to
It will be flooded by rising sea levels
Methane is toxic to alpine plants
markScheme: 1 mark: its habitat moves uphill and there is nowhere higher to go
questions.explanation: Cold-adapted species near summits lose their habitat as it shifts upwards. Sea level rise does not affect mountain tops.

questions.question: Why are scientists' predictions about the effects of global warming on species uncertain?
options: Scientists do not collect any data
Global warming is not happening
Only one scientist has studied it
The climate and ecosystems are complex systems with many interacting factors
markScheme: 1 mark: complex systems with many interacting factors
questions.explanation: There is a large body of peer-reviewed evidence for global warming, but complex systems make exact predictions difficult.

Calculate how many times faster the mean rate of increase was from 2010 to 2020 than from 1960 to 1970.
markScheme: 1 mark: rates are 0.9 ppm per year and 2.4 ppm per year
questions.explanation: 1960 to 1970: 9 ÷ 10 = 0.9 ppm per year. 2010 to 2020: 24 ÷ 10 = 2.4 ppm per year. 2.4 ÷ 0.9 = 2.67, so the rate was about 2.7 times faster.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the mean date a bird species arrived at a nature reserve in 1970 and in 2020.
Calculate the mean change in arrival date per decade.
markScheme: 1 mark: change = 12 days over 50 years (5 decades)
1 mark: 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4 days earlier per decade
questions.explanation: From 20 April to 8 April is 12 days. 50 years is 5 decades, so the arrival date became 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4 days earlier per decade.

questions.question: Name the two gases whose levels in the atmosphere are increasing and contributing to global warming.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide
1 mark: methane
questions.explanation: Both gases are greenhouse gases whose levels are increasing.

questions.question: Give one source of the extra methane in the atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: cattle / rice fields / landfill
questions.explanation: Cattle release methane during digestion; microorganisms in rice fields and landfill sites also release methane.

questions.question: Explain how global warming could lead to the loss of habitats in low-lying coastal areas.
markScheme: 1 mark: ice (on land) melts and sea water expands, so sea levels rise
1 mark: low-lying areas are flooded, so organisms living there lose their habitat
questions.explanation: The causal chain is warming, then melting and expansion, then sea level rise, then flooding of habitats.

questions.question: Describe two biological consequences of global warming, other than sea level rise.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: changes in distribution of species; changes in migration patterns; reduced biodiversity or extinctions; spread of pests or disease vectors; changes in the timing of flowering or breeding
questions.explanation: Any two distinct biological consequences gain credit.

questions.question: Explain how an increase in temperature could change the distribution of a species.
markScheme: 1 mark: the area where it lives becomes too warm (or rainfall changes), so the species cannot survive or reproduce there
1 mark: cooler areas (towards the poles or higher up) become suitable, so the species is found there instead
questions.explanation: Distribution changes as populations decline where conditions become unsuitable and increase where they become suitable.

questions.question: A species of bird times its breeding so that its chicks hatch when caterpillars are most common. Due to warmer springs, the caterpillars now reach their peak two weeks earlier, but the birds still breed at the same time. Suggest and explain the effect on the bird population.
markScheme: 1 mark: chicks hatch after the peak in caterpillars
1 mark: so there is less food for the chicks
1 mark: fewer chicks survive, so the bird population decreases
questions.explanation: A mismatch in timing between a predator and its prey reduces the food available when it is most needed.

questions.question: Most scientists agree that global warming is linked to human activity. Suggest why this agreement is considered to be reliable.
markScheme: 1 mark: based on a very large number of studies or data from many sources (temperature records, ice cores, CO₂ measurements)
1 mark: the research has been peer reviewed / repeated by many independent scientists
questions.explanation: A conclusion supported by many independent, peer-reviewed studies is much more reliable than one based on a single study.

questions.question: Describe how human activities have increased the levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere.
markScheme: Indicative content: carbon dioxide: burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) in power stations, vehicles and homes; deforestation: burning trees, decay of wood by microorganisms, less photosynthesis; destruction of peat bogs (decay or burning of peat); methane: cattle farming, rice fields, decaying waste in landfill sites; growing population and higher standard of living increase these activities.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of sources of both gases, with at least two sources each or explanation of how they release the gas.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements naming one or two sources.
questions.explanation: A good answer deals with both gases separately and gives specific activities.

questions.question:
Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing.
Describe the biological consequences of global warming for organisms and ecosystems.
markScheme: Indicative content: carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases contributing to global warming; ice melts and sea level rises, flooding low-lying habitats (saltmarshes, mangroves, islands), loss of habitat; loss of sea ice affects polar species; changes in temperature and rainfall change the distribution of species, shifting towards poles or uphill; cold-adapted species lose habitat; warm-adapted species, pests and disease vectors spread into new areas; changes in migration patterns (earlier arrival, different routes, no migration); changes in timing of breeding or flowering causing mismatches in food chains; coral bleaching; species that cannot adapt or move become extinct; biodiversity reduced; effects on food chains and food production.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed and well-linked description of several consequences, including loss of habitat, changes in distribution and migration patterns, and reduced biodiversity, with clear cause and effect.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several consequences described with some links to the cause.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two simple consequences, for example 'animals lose their homes'.
questions.explanation: High-scoring answers explain each consequence as a chain of cause and effect and finish with the overall effect on biodiversity.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes how deforestation increases the level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
options: Fewer trees means less carbon dioxide is removed by photosynthesis
Trees release methane when cut down
Cut trees absorb more carbon dioxide
Soil releases oxygen after deforestation
markScheme: 1 mark: fewer trees, less photosynthesis, less carbon dioxide removed
questions.explanation: Trees remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis. Burning and decay of the wood also release carbon dioxide.

questions.question: State what happens to the average temperature of the Earth when the levels of greenhouse gases increase.
markScheme: 1 mark: it increases
questions.explanation: More greenhouse gases contribute to global warming, an increase in the Earth's average surface temperature.

questions.question: Coral reefs have high biodiversity. Sea temperature rises cause coral bleaching, which can kill corals. What is the most likely effect on the reef ecosystem?
options: Biodiversity increases because there is more space
Only the coral is affected
Fish populations increase because there are fewer corals
Many species that depend on coral for food and shelter decline, so biodiversity falls
markScheme: 1 mark: species depending on coral decline, so biodiversity falls
questions.explanation: Corals provide food and shelter for many reef species, so their death has knock-on effects through the ecosystem.
